case_info.explanation: Seven months after initial presentation, findings of a lumbar puncture were normal with no malignant cells identified, and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoproliferative disorder. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography found no distinct hypermetabolism. Serum studies indicated mildly elevated IgG4, beta-2-microglobulin, and lactate dehydrogenase. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. This mutational signature is typically associated with UV-induced DNA damage, suggesting an SCC of cutaneous rather than mucosal head and neck origin.1The patient was diagnosed with recurrent cSCC with perineural tumor spread (PNTS), which was surgically unresectable and unsuitable for curative-intent radiotherapy due to extensive involvement of CN5 and CN7. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. PNTS from cSCC often involves CN5 and CN7, mimicking benign facial numbness and weakness. The concurrence of CN5 and CN7 deficits in patients with a history of NMSC should raise suspicion for PNTS. Tumor spread between these nerves occurs at specific sites, including the sphenopalatine ganglion, the lingual nerve-chorda tympani junction, and the auriculotemporal nerve.3The auriculotemporal nerve, a V3 branch, connects to CN7 in the retromandibular region and supplies sensation to the preauricular skin and external ear, explaining this patient’s symptoms. For cSCC unsuitable for curative surgery or radiation, anti–programmed cell death 1 protein checkpoint inhibitors are the standard of care, offering high response rates.4This patient received cemiplimab for 6 months, showing radiographic tumor regression without major immune-related adverse effects but persistent neuropathies, including complete left facial weakness. Facial reanimation surgery was performed to restore facial movements. Consolidation radiation therapy to residual disease along CN5 and CN7 was recommended alongside maintenance immunotherapy. PNTS to cranial nerves can be misdiagnosed as Bell palsy, a term often used for postviral neuropathies. However, PNTS should be considered in patients with a history of facial or scalp premalignant or malignant lesions, especially if symptoms persist or worsen despite corticosteroids. One review reported a median 6-month delay from symptom onset to diagnosis.5Timely referral to specialized centers is critical. MRI protocols optimized for cranial nerve imaging are essential for diagnosis, as early PNTS may be radiographically occult. Serial MRIs and targeted nerve biopsies help confirm the diagnosis, though biopsies may not always be feasible. Awareness of cSCC’s potential spread to CN5 and CN7 is vital for early detection and treatment, preventing diagnostic delays.

case_info.explanation: Seven months after initial presentation, findings of a lumbar puncture were normal with no malignant cells identified, and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoproliferative disorder. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography found no distinct hypermetabolism. Serum studies indicated mildly elevated IgG4, beta-2-microglobulin, and lactate dehydrogenase. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. This mutational signature is typically associated with UV-induced DNA damage, suggesting an SCC of cutaneous rather than mucosal head and neck origin.1The patient was diagnosed with recurrent cSCC with perineural tumor spread (PNTS), which was surgically unresectable and unsuitable for curative-intent radiotherapy due to extensive involvement of CN5 and CN7. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. PNTS from cSCC often involves CN5 and CN7, mimicking benign facial numbness and weakness. The concurrence of CN5 and CN7 deficits in patients with a history of NMSC should raise suspicion for PNTS. Tumor spread between these nerves occurs at specific sites, including the sphenopalatine ganglion, the lingual nerve-chorda tympani junction, and the auriculotemporal nerve.3The auriculotemporal nerve, a V3 branch, connects to CN7 in the retromandibular region and supplies sensation to the preauricular skin and external ear, explaining this patient’s symptoms. For cSCC unsuitable for curative surgery or radiation, anti–programmed cell death 1 protein checkpoint inhibitors are the standard of care, offering high response rates.4This patient received cemiplimab for 6 months, showing radiographic tumor regression without major immune-related adverse effects but persistent neuropathies, including complete left facial weakness. Facial reanimation surgery was performed to restore facial movements. Consolidation radiation therapy to residual disease along CN5 and CN7 was recommended alongside maintenance immunotherapy. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. This mutational signature is typically associated with UV-induced DNA damage, suggesting an SCC of cutaneous rather than mucosal head and neck origin.1The patient was diagnosed with recurrent cSCC with perineural tumor spread (PNTS), which was surgically unresectable and unsuitable for curative-intent radiotherapy due to extensive involvement of CN5 and CN7. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC.
